fatal_errors: The proposed spark plasma sintering route is not the target liquid-metal dealloying process involving immersion of directionally segregated WTaVTi in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h.

The hypothesis incorrectly treats rapid densification and unspecified in-situ reinforcing phases as the solution; the target mechanism is selective Ti–Cu exchange followed by formation of a W-rich passivating interlayer.

The cited evidence concerns a Cu-free NbMoCrTiAl composite reinforced with TiC and Al2O3, so it does not support compatibility, reaction, or microstructural stability between Cu and refractory elements.
The proposed approximately 1700 °C SPS conditions and powder precursor do not reproduce the target precursor morphology or the directional, bicontinuous RHEA–Cu architecture.
The predicted outcomes omit the defining thermal-conductivity enhancement, aligned Cu transport channels, W-rich interface, and qualified helium-irradiation result.
explanation: The response recognizes the broad challenge of combining Cu with a refractory high-entropy alloy, but reconstructs a fundamentally different material, processing route, mechanism, and microstructure. The hidden work uses liquid-metal dealloying of an as-cast, directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor, exploiting preferential dissolution of Ti-rich interdendritic channels into molten Cu. This produces continuous Cu channels, retained BCC RHEA ligaments, and an approximately 300 nm W-rich interfacial layer that passivates the interface. By contrast, the generated hypothesis assumes mechanically alloyed powders, SPS densification, and unspecified ceramic or intermetallic reinforcement. Its sole citation establishes SPS reinforcement in a Cu-free NbMoCrTiAl–TiC–Al2O3 system and therefore cannot validate the central Cu–RHEA claim. The proposed experiment is measurable and could falsify the SPS hypothesis, but comparing Cu-containing and Cu-free SPS samples would not directly test whether SPS overcomes Cu–refractory immiscibility or distinguish the claimed reinforcement mechanism from simple densification and segregation effects.
